blocks.x: I was in Barnes on 1889. What was the birth date exactly?
January of the 18th.
That's all, only strictly music.
We just played at the country club. We got all high class jobs. You see like coming around Carnival time now, we have all them Carnival boys at A&M, different places like that. Country club.
About what date was that, in the 1920s, along and after the war?
That was between 23 and, between 23 and 27, around in there.
Did you keep a book on all of those dates too? No, no, no. I saw your little book about Chris's band one day.

I only had them little yearly books and put it on every day. They had to do that to keep them being confused. Sure. Otherwise, we were getting so many jobs that if you didn't have them on the book, you were, you get a job like you're playing now, you get a job for next week sometime where you're marked at. You get a job like that, you see? Then I would mark the price what I'd get for a two. I don't know. I played with Robichaux. Now we used to play at the country club on Saturday night. On Sundays, we'd get on a boat, we'd call the Susquehanna. We would go over the manoeuvre, over the lake. We'd just take them over there and we'd hang around all day and just bring them back.
You'd play on the boat over there too or just on the boat?
Just on the boat. Just on the boat. We'd be free to loaf around.
You'd have dancing on the boat too?

Oh yeah. Then we had, through the week we had excursions on the lake on the same boat. I just remember what night, but it was two nights we used to have excursions on the Susquehanna. Way out there, it was just as cool out there on the lake. Way out on the lake you could see the lights, you know, the guard light.
How long did it take the boat to get across the lake then?

It was about an hour, an hour and a half at that time. One hour and a half, you could say one hour, it was pretty fast. Yeah, fast. And we used to play out on the, every night on the, go out on an excursion and play. And come in, come back and you could hear the band playing at the night clubs after we'd get back, you see. And you could hear us, used to have a band near where the boat landed called...
Where did that land, at West End or Spanish Fort, about where?
West End.
West End.

Uh huh, used to leave from West End. And, uh, had a band. It had, different places have three or four pieces band in it. You know, it was, always was nice out there. And they used to have the hour band, or that was a big band like ours. They used to, used to be playing in a club out there too. And when we'd be coming, coming home or coming along after we'd get off the boat, we could hear them playing. It's a good band too.
Did they play at the Southern Yacht Club, was that, or where?
Oh, they wasn't at the, at the Yacht Club then. There's some club they used to play every night.
Right at West End?

West End Roof, wasn't it? Huh? West End Roof, wasn't it? I think it was. I think that's the name of it. They had so many different places I'd get confused if I'm trying to take a show. Yeah, anyway, West End. Yeah, there's a player there, and they used to come on. They still sound good on that water, at night in band, that music still sound nice out there. Late at night, you know. And you could play too. They could play. We'd come on in. We'd catch a call right there in the West End call and bring us in town. And we was playing at Antoine one night. We used to play a big dance there, you know. And we had ten pieces that night. Yeah, Robeshow got a couple more other pieces. And we was playing there. And a fella come and asked for a piece of music. And Robeshow, he had a big bundle of music. He went down there and got a couple of pieces out. The man said, he said, take a look at it. We're going to play that next piece. The man, he told the man, first he told the man, I'll look and see if I got it. You know, he had so many he couldn't remember himself. So he had it. And he put it up there. And we started off. It's nice. And ten piece of band, you know, I thought I could hide, you know. Sometime you can get by on certain things, but you keep your eye on that music, you know. And if they get too hard for you, you kind of get over that and catch the next, you know. So I played that night and there was a party in there for the trambones, you know. And that's the first time I'd seen the piece of music. So when I got there, I missed it. Of course the fellas in the band, I don't guess they know the difference, you know. So, alright, you have to come back, play the encoder, play it again. I missed it again. I missed it. It's a, it's a, it's a very, it teaches a piece of music. But they never know, you see. So when I finished, a fella came up to me and said, that's a nice piece you all played. I said, yeah. He said, you missed something in there, didn't you? I said, I sure did.
You knew the piece, huh?
Yeah, you know. You know who it was when I come to find out? It was a fella that played in that hour band.
Oh, right.

But I had been hearing it. He's good, too. He's good. He said, well I'll tell you, he said, that piece give me some. He said, I'd listen for you to come out and see if you missed it. He said, I'll miss it, too. And I thought he'd get it down, you know. I thought he got it down and he'd miss it too.
This is the first time you ever saw it. You did pretty good to keep going.
Yeah. When you're playing like that, if you can keep up with the music, you skip. If you miss, yeah, don't miss over there. If you get out, you're out altogether, you see.
This was a, was this Neto? Was that his name? Who? Neto, the trombone player was out. I think it was, yeah.
Now he was a guest at that. He had on his tuxedos and everything. He was a guest at that day.
When you played at Ambrons there, was that for a sort of a private party or was it the regular dinner or what?
No, that's private.
They didn't have a band every night? No.

Not our band. No, I don't think. They're special. And at that dance, we was a play to one and the phone hired us an hour over. We was getting from ten to one. We sat at ten, play to one, that was, we was getting ten dollars for that job.
How big a place now, they have five or six dining rooms all over that whole block they took over about. But how many dining rooms did they have in those days? Was it a big place then upstairs?

Well, I'll tell you, we was in a certain place, we didn't even see the waiter or the kitchen where we were that night. We was in a place like where we played, we couldn't see the kitchen, or neither, where they were only dancing, there wasn't no dining.
Yeah.
They must have dined in other place because they had their little hats on and things like that, but they would dance where the, where we were sitting, we just could see the dances.

I wanted to ask some more about the plantation down there. We talked to Sonny Henry a couple weeks ago. He couldn't remember who else was in the band. He said you'd know all of those fellas. You told us about your three brothers and you. Yeah. Do you remember who else? Some of the men.
Whenever they get the brothers' names. I know all the men that are in there, but they're not living.
Well, if you know their names, then your names are your brothers too.
You want to know that too?
It would be nice to have them, yes.
Thomas Bonds was the oldest.
Were they still living? Any of your brothers living?
No, they're all down. Thomas Bonds was the oldest. Freddie Bonds.
How much older was the oldest brother than you?
Just about three years different. Freddie Bonds was the second. Then Alfred Bonds. Then I had a sister. Well, she's older than I am. It was four boys and one girl. Did she play any instrument?
No, she didn't. Piano, guitar, nothing like that?
No, she wasn't. And I was the last. We were about three years apart. My oldest brother might have been about fifteen years, fourteen, fifteen years older than me, you know.
What instruments did they play that? Thomas played what?
E-flat clarinet.
And Freddie? Huh? And Freddie Bonds? Baritone.

Alfred Bonds played E-flat clarinet. Now we went to play. We went up about four miles from home to a little dance. And they had a little orchestra there. Playing, you know. And my brothers say, think we can play a little bit? Them fellas? Well, they said, that couldn't be, you know. That was a C, you know, that was a C, C tram on, built-in C, what he had. And my brother plays with an E-flat clarinet. This fella had a B-flat clarinet. And they wanted Charlie McCurdy's, I mean, not Charlie McCurdy's. And now the fella, he's a kind of professor in there. And they got there and he explained to them, see, that wouldn't sound good like that. See, it wouldn't, you couldn't make it, you see. And I had the trumpet, you know, and I was playing the trumpet, so. What I did, see y'all, see how, I said, let's see how y'all were playing. Now when they played, they correspond, you see. Now, the way I played, I couldn't correspond, you see. That trumpet had B and A, you see.
Yeah, it was rolling with G's right there.
Yeah, it had the B and A. So, don't you know how I played that trumpet in there?
You did it anyway, huh?
I played it in tune too, you know, yeah. You know what I had to do? I had them prices there already on my trumpet. You see, I picked that third vowel on the trumpet and put it down.
Kept it down all the time? Kept it down.

Kept it down. That put my, that, that throwed my, my instrument in A. Mm-hmm. And I played, played them out just like this. How did they do it like that? Now when I, when I get to the place where I had to use a third vowel, I let it up. And that man, they don't know today how I could play, how I made that to play that.
They don't know.
But I did it. Good. From experience, yeah, yeah. Well, uh. I hold that third vowel down, that third man and A and I played along with, it first morning with them.
Well, I think of it, after we talked to Sonny Henry, the next day we saw him, he said, Oh, I forgot to tell you about the big bell or something down at Magnolia.
Or did he go, used to go to work? I don't know what it was, he didn't tell us.
He said he forgot to tell us on the big plantation bell.
Oh yeah, he got a big bell that sets up on like a tower. And they would ring one about, in the summertime, they'd ring a bell about, about 4 or 4.15 in the morning.
In the morning, is that right?

Yeah, in the morning, it was daylight. It's now daylight, it'd be daylight around, 4.30 is putting that daylight. Then they'd ring the others around, but, but, about 15 minutes apart anyhow, they'd ring, they used to call it the first bell and the second bell. And A and A gets up there and go ahead and go around the stable and get the mule and then get on out there. Sometime when you get out of there and be going out there, you'll be near to your work, a mile, sometime a half a mile, the sun don't just be peeping up sometime. But the gladdest sun in the morning is day, but the sun don't be up. You can see the rays of it coming up. And you start out there and then around about 7 o'clock or 7.30, a boy would bring you breakfast. A fellow with a water boy, he's bringing breakfast out there. And you'd have it half an hour, sit down, eat breakfast, and you'd get up and go again. Maybe 11 o'clock when the sun hot, you knock off around about 11 o'clock, you know. You go home, you come out about 1 or 1.30, you come back. And then you'd have to tell it about 6.30.
Did they ring a bell at noon all the time for that too?

They had a bell at noon, yeah. All the time. You didn't need to be right up on the pump with the bell, you know. See, when the bell rings, you'll be home. That didn't mean for you to come to work. It didn't mean for you to go, be on the job at the bell, you know. You leave home. Well, I used to like my daddy. He was a foreman, you know. And when I was young, younger all my brothers' wife was giving their money to my daddy. So they built a house, place, and thing just about a mile and a half from there. And my brother went and lived over there. One of the oldest brothers, he made chalk and fish, you see, and trap.
What kind of work did you have to do on the plantation? Was it all sugar or what down there? On the plantation?
Well, it's… I was one of the first-class men out there. How much do you reckon they gave me more than the other men? Nickel.
Nickel. They didn't get 80 cents a day.
They didn't get 80 cents a day.
I did a day, not an hour.

They was getting 80 cents a day. And I was getting 85 cents a day. I had about seven or eight of us making that kind of money, you see. That is, when they get the new ground, it doesn't hire it off level. You know how they hire it. Yeah. Well, now you had to make rows. And making them rows, it had to be sight and distant apart. And you take your measuring stick and you put it down. And you have sticks, you know, to make that row straight, you had a couple of sticks that away. And you had to keep it right straight. You call that laying off rows. And you had to go right straight to that stick. When you get to that stick, you stop and you take it over. You lay down for the next row. You understand? That's when bring it back. Or you call that laying off rows. And if you wasn't good on that, when they would get to a ditch bank or something like that, if you didn't go straight, you'd have short rows that come in there on you. So to keep them rows level, you had to have it straight. Sometime you got to know how to take a little bit off with this. Little bit by little bit. Little by little, if you get out of the way a little bit, you got to eat your back. And they never could tell the difference. So then what's called first class men, we used to do that. And on the plantation, otherwise, where you just had ordinary work, we had a machine that we could set up on all day. The cultivators and things, we just set up on wheels and ride. Different machine. Then we had one, used to run with three wheels. You straddle the row and had two discs on each side. And this throw on each side and you had to guide it like that in the mule. I used to love it. Didn't know no better, you see. And they sold that plantation. They sold that plantation. The governor came around and recommended the boss to the fellas, you know. Said this is going to be the next man to take their place. And I'd like for you all to work for him. And just like he did for me. He was a fine man and everything. And they got to me and said, what you say about it? And I said, well, I can't promise you. And I said, I don't think, I couldn't promise you I'm going to be here. So, I went to work when the man was taking it over the first of the year. And it was during February. Everything was going pretty good. We were, cane rows where we were throwing that dirt down from the cane rows. And he was going to make rice, you see. And one day it was coming with rain. It rained all night. And that morning I was laying in bed. A fellow that was foaming at the time come around and called me. He said, I know. I said, why? They're going to work this morning? He said, why? I said, man. I said, it rained all night. I said, how you going to work? Well, in the cane farm you didn't work, you know. Rice you needed to work. Too wet. He said, it's the rice field now, man. He said, it's just right now. I said, what?
I said, no.

I said, well, I don't want to be contrary, you know. Be the contrary one. I said, well, I'll go. I didn't like it. I got up. And I went out there and they had water laying in the middle, you see. Water on this side and water on that side. Because the road, well, they didn't have, wasn't covered. I got that applied. I didn't like, I didn't like that water. I wasn't used to getting that water. And the mules, they didn't like it. They would knock one another on the side, you know. They keep them walking on the water and push them back on their side. And I'm back there. And I had to plow with one hand, trying to keep my foot out of the water. But I know, when you're, you have to get wet. Yeah. You had to get in that water. I made that day. I came home and I had $40 saved up. I told my mother, I said, I ain't going back here. I ain't going out there anymore. I gave her 20 of the dollars that I had. I got a freight train that passes, you know. And I know they were all the fellas on there, so. You could work your way on the, on the, on the, work your way to the city, you see. If you'd go down and, and you come back, you can go on to the city with them. You're working your way. You wouldn't have to pee. So I told them to have my clothes out of them when I, when I passed back. And they had them out there and I came on the city and I've been there ever since.
What happened to that plantation? Was there a break in the levee? I believe the study or somebody told it, it's washed out now. Was there water over that or what happened down there?
I went down there about, about three months ago. And I hadn't been down there for years. And I hardly know the place when I got there. Growing up in weeds and grass. Not much there.
No. Well what happened to Deer Range?
That's the place that went underwater I guess.
That's the place where the water was. Yeah.
We're talking Deer Range around there. That's something, they still have the, the land is still down with Magnolia. Yeah.
Yeah. Was there ever a big plantation house? Is it still there? Well yeah, the, the one that the governor used to live in, you know, this night, this was

put up, it's, it's still there I think. Oh yeah. Uh. But the other places, it ain't got no landmark at all. Yeah. The old landmark is gone. Did any city bands ever come down to Magnolia, the Montana Hill? No.
No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.
No. No. No. No.
No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. We had a little country band, but I thought that was the best band that they had.
Who was in Henry Allen's band then? Did you know the fellows in Henry Allen's band?
They're putting it all night out.
We want you to speak for them. They can't speak for themselves, so you tell us who some of them were.

He had his brother. His brother used to be a beat snare drum. Used to have a fellow beat bass drum. They called him Yance. Well, you wouldn't know the name. Their name wouldn't... What's his name? They used to call him Yance. That's the kind of Creole name. He got plenty of people around him.
Was he there before Clay Giles was playing bass drum?
Oh, that's a different band altogether. That's an extensive band.
Oh, I thought Clay Giles played with Allen at one time.

Not that I know of. Not that I know of. He wasn't there. When I know John, he was playing with the Excelsior. And I was playing with the Excelsior. A fellow by the name of Yance was beatin' drum. Bass drum.
Does that mean anything? That name Yance? Does it have any meaning?
Yance?
Mm-hmm.

No, there isn't. You know all them Creole people, all them funny names. I just don't mean nothing. Not that I know of. I know his people. They had plenty of fellas out there. Old musicians, you see. They were... I was living in the country then. Mm-hmm. The time I'm telling you what, when they come out there. And when I come here, well, they had done this band.
You remember Frankie Doosen ever went down in the country that way? Did you work with him?
He was playing with Allen, too. He was one of the fellas playing with Allen at that time.
Did he ever come down there in a dance band or anything?
No, I never seen him in a dance band, but I came up here and hear them play in a dance band. At the...
Do you remember ever hearing Willie Farnish in a dance band down there in the country anywhere else?

No, I heard him up here. I heard him up here. I didn't hear him, no. I needed to do it. The only... We didn't have no big dances at my home. The Excursion bands used to come out there. You see, when they had the band Excursion, that's the only big band. Sometimes White would come by there, too. I heard a band playing... The first time I heard that was a long time ago.
Alexander's Right Time Band?

Yeah, and I loved Liza, you know, and they played that about... You see, they take water at the place where it was. And I went up and I said, what's the name of that piece? He told me. Alexander Right Time Band. And that ain't been the date. That's an old number. That's an old number.
Do you remember a carnet player, Buddy Bolden? Did he ever get down there on excursion or anything?

Not that I know of. Bolden was on his way out when I got here. I heard him several times. He used to go around by the... He used to have a square right where the auditorium is now. That square that used to go straight across, used to be named Congo Square, the changes to Burgard Square. And they had a hall that's called the Globe Hall right there. Where you could sit down out in the square, when they're going to have a dance there, they'll come outside and play two, three numbers. That's where I heard Bolden, some Manuel Perez, all different bands would come around. They would get out and play a couple of numbers. Franky Dusen.
Did you hear Bolden after you moved up here or did you come up here on a visit sometime before...
On a visit.
On a visit.
Yeah. And he had a couple of pieces he made famous notes that put on record and things like that. Just called them Bolden. So we, our Magnolia band came up here and played, played a parade, you know?
What you did up here in the city?
And all the fellas used to give a layout every, around the 10th of May every year. Used to call it the 10th of May anyhow.
Yeah, I heard of those.
And they had our band came up. And we didn't even have uniform at that time. Well we got white coats, you know?
Yeah.

Just had a white coat and white cap. You could get a cap for 25 cents at that time, for that last year's day. Things was cheap. And my drum player, the bass drum player had to get a pair of tennis shoes like, you know? Black one, like that. His feet was hiding him and he had tennis shoes to make that parade. And then we went on that parade and all them bands, big bands, well we didn't think, we thought our band was the least on that, you know? And we went to playin' that day and they used to make some long parades. Just start around 8 o'clock, 9 o'clock and play until 5 and 6 o'clock in the evening. So we played and played. We'd see musicians got burnt out, you know? And setten out. That same son of Henry said, man, I'm gonna quit. I said, man, look at that man. One fella dropped dead, you see?
Who was that?
There was a fella who used to play, he's from this side too. He was playing with Allen, I think. He was playing with Allen's band. On that play?
Yeah, trumpet.
Well, I guess maybe it might have been heart trouble or something else, you know? Someone like, when Walter Blue, when did he die?
I'm trying to remember.
Did you say Chris Kelly was with you at that time too? Was he playing with the Magnolia band?
No, no, no, no, no, no.
That was before he was right before his time?
No, he wasn't playing at all at that time, you see? By me being right there, he used to live just on this side of us, you see? He was about six miles above, but we know one another, you know?
Yeah, he doesn't belong to the Magnolia band.

No, no, he wasn't living right there on that plantation. He was living in a place where they arranged. Yeah. What they call it, they arranged now, that's where Chris was. And of course, he probably didn't have music on his mind at that time.
I interrupted you about your time about that parade though, that you played the 10th of May parade.

Yeah, we played and when we got, they said, we passed around and one of the ladies said, where did that fellas come from? Where's them white coats? You know when you passed, they did have different cracks, you see? Yeah. And they got on, got on time, they had a, what they call a district. That is where they got a... Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
You were talking about your white coats in the van there again.
Yeah.
And it went through the district, you said.

Through the district? Yeah. Now, we had done been made around all uptown, coming down, you know. And we had passed, we were coming through the district. That is, around Franklin Street and things. I mean, they had a place between Franklin and St. Louis. They'd run dead into the cemetery, like, you know. Around in there was all fast people, you know. You used to call it the district. So, we was coming through there late that evening, you see. Different bands had what, maybe 16, 17 bands. All they could get, they had to go in the country and get us, you know. They had money. So, we came, coming through there, we played a piece. What Bowling had made famous, you know. I don't know the name of it. How does it go? And we strong on them trumpet, too, me and my cousin, you know. And them women come out and say, yeah, come Bowling Band. They just clap for us, you know. And they just run out and say, that must be Bowling Band. Right? Our country was strong, you know. And the whole other fellas here in the city was falling out and things. We used to being in that sunny thing out there, flowering and things. We strong. We went on too.
Is that the same piece that Bowling played that you played it, you say?
Yeah. We played that in the country, yeah. You had the music for it?
No, no music.
You just had it. Yeah, just by air. You see, just catch them things by air. Daylight the Air. I don't remember that tune. What is it?
Sing a little more of it. Maybe I've heard it. I don't remember it, though. I don't think you heard that tune.
It was a very famous rhyme.
It was very nice.

Yeah. That was the cornet part you were humming? Yeah. Must be Don't Go Away Nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That was the cornet part you were humming? Yeah. Must be Don't Go Away Nobody, huh? It was centric too. It was centric too. It was centric too. give the tone, some of them was pretty nice pieces.
Like a blues? Huh? Like a blues, you see what it?

I mean, the band used to make their own name for the pieces. See, just like Lewis and them used to make it, called it Gut Bucket and all different kind of funny names. They had to have a name, so they just called it that name, but it was never published. You know what I'm saying? It was never published, the name or nothing. So we made a hit. And the people gave us a big hand, that band from the country, and they had a band from St. John Parish. They were good, too, at that time. I believe you should call them the Pickwick or something like that. It was pretty good. It was really nice. And the year before that, they had made a piece by the name of Howl Arthur. They made a hit with that. They had to play that. It was in the paper, you know? They played it about 20 times or something like that. It was in the daily paper. Is that there?
Is that there?

Is it Lizard on the Rail? Is that what I'm saying? Yeah, yeah, yeah. That's the Howl Arthur is the name of it. They just put an ad voice to it. Yeah, yeah, Lizard on the Rail. With his tail. Yeah, they made it. That's one of the Jim Mumford band he had up there, too. They made good, that was before we came in.

Oh, talking about Frankie Dooson, somebody told us that he used to go down in the country, I believe on the other side of the river, and taught some of the bands, like Sam Morgan's band or something. Did you ever hear of Frankie Dooson teaching anybody or going around? He didn't know nothing about music itself.

I wonder, too, somebody told me he couldn't read. I wonder how he could go around and teach a band. It's wrong, it's wrong. The last place I played with him, I don't know, I went in, of course we had a project band, we used to call it WPA band, you know? And he was in there when he was signed up and was in there before I was. I went in there front of me, and he was just blind as he ever was, around that line. He couldn't, he couldn't read.
Do you remember who else was with Bolden when you heard him in Globe Hall? Did you know any of the other men?

Connish used to play time on with him at the time. I don't know none of the other fellas, but I don't know none of the other fellas. I may not know one of them after, but I don't know whether they didn't tell me whether they were with him because I know a good many old musicians.
Well, was he out that day when you played his tune?
Was he on the street? No, no, he was past, I think he had quit at that time. So, shortly after or before that, once he had kind of lost his mind.
Did you ever play in the same band with him ever?

No, no, no. I don't know him too good, but I've heard him when I used to be in the park. See, I didn't come here until 1930, and he's famous around from 1910 to 1912, like that. You couldn't hear nothing but Buddy Bolden. You see, he was one of the old musicians, and he was famous, you see. He was strong, and he'd make up his own tone. Well, there's something different that people would be after. You see, you take like Manuel Perez, well, he was more of a music man. He had a pretty good band. He was, he wasn't after that race, he wasn't much on that race. I mean, strong man, but he's a music man.
You mentioned they wrote up in the paper about the Pickwick band. Did you ever see any pictures of the old bands in the paper, or did anybody have pictures like Bolden of those old bands?
Not that I know of.
Did anybody ever take a picture of your Magnolia band down in the country? A photograph, anything?

Oh, we got plenty of them that it was taken down whilst we was home, you know. People, sometimes we'd go out to the train. You see, in a country like that, in the aisle like that, we just parade around the street. And we'd go out when the train come to take water there, you know. They'd be, say, there about 10 minutes, we'd bear a couple of tones like that. Some people would snap them. And right on the place, they used to snap us every time we'd have a big out. And people would snap what the, there never was no pictures delivered to us.
We'd never, never, never had any of those pictures.
Any pictures of Chris Kelly around?
No.
I guess Ben Kelly's still alive.
He's still alive, yeah.
Well, that's drag. He may know where. Or his song. He's still alive.

Was there much difference in the style of the band, the brass band up here in the city? Before they got tired and wore out, did they play more head music or read all the time? Was there much difference in your band and the other bands?

Well, I think the country band was the best. Because they had fellas, they would pick up men, different men in some of these bands. And they wasn't good as the band just had a big name. Yeah, that's right. The band just had a big name and that's all. And the fellas from the country, they learned that off the cards, what they had, they know it. And they wasn't going to play no more than what was written there. See?
And yet you played some head things like that, tuned there.

Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, we'd get together on that, you see. We'd get together on that and prices that and they're going to play it that way. Yeah. See now, I had a cousin playing trumpet with me. He was pretty good on making the mixture notes in there, you see. And I was pretty good too to fill in, you see, you know. Yeah. To make it sound good. So. No. I used to think the fellas here was way above us. And I didn't find out until I got in the WPA band. And they come down where they had to put that music up there and I had much chance at them, you see.
Yeah.

They ain't know nothing. I had to teach them. The fella come in the X7 band. He was, I used to think he was a great man. The fella in the Georgia Hooker. He used to play trumpet in the band over here, the Pacific band. I thought he was a big shot. He had them on baritone and come over there and had to show them how to divide the music. Well, I was surprised. Then they hired me from the country to play with a, Sonny Henry recommended me to a band, they call it the Terramir band, down in Ninth Wall. They come up here and play a parade with them. He said, Sonny Henry said, you send the music out there. I said, that fella will be alright. So they sent the music about a week ahead of time, you know. They had me on what you call the second carnage. They had first and second, you know. They had me on second carnage parts. So I went over them and there was nothing too hard, you know. They had a few marches there, but I got them down good. They had one of them marches called Old Faithful. So I came up here that Sunday to rehearse with the band to go out that Monday. And I got up, we was down in the night one night. We was playing down there and rehearsing. I know mine, already had mine down. So the same, George Hooker, he came over. He must have heard they were rehearsing down there. He came over and brought a few, a few of his pieces, you know. Come down there, we was rehearsing. He come down there and, you know, I got some pieces, you know, I want you all to look over. They had a trumpet player playing the rest, a couple of them. As soon as he come in there and put that down, they come and it's going out of one, I want to go in the back so well, you know. So I look at it and I look at it. I said, all right. So two or three of us just run over it, you know. We wasn't going to play that the next day, no harm, but we just, and I played it and I played it pretty good, you know. I found out it did well. They found out it was good. I wouldn't run. So when, after he played that piece, we played that piece, I said, we going to play this and put it, we had the old faithful, you know. Even on the back, run here. I said, he wouldn't play that. And I said, he brought that here for the fellas and he ran in there. So I didn't find out he couldn't, he wasn't that old until he come in the accepted band. After I had come back here to town, I found out all the musicians. And when I got in the WPA band, what we call a WPA band, I don't know who this is. So they had 20 chime on players in there. They about to have about 100 altogether, maybe more, under the instrument. So Frankie Dewson was, had the lead cheer, you know. And when he seen me, he said, you take the lead. I said, no, you stay where you are. You want me to take the lead cheer? I said, I'll set any place to see it, it didn't make no reason to me, because the music wasn't all that hard. And we played around and they had nothing too hard to play. So the fellow, what we playing for, after we played with a Montessori, he said, they're going to have a test, you know.
Who was the leader, the boss of the whole band?

A fellow by the name of Mr. Gilbert, you know. He had it in charge, so he said he's going to run a test. He run a test. He was going to run a test. And put the music up, you know. And the music wasn't all that hard. And a whole lot of fellows couldn't make, didn't know nothing at all. And a week or so they cut the band down to about 70-something. They stayed in on trombone. Frankie Duesen still there? They passed him some kind of way they liked him, you know. Then again, Frankie Bluffey, if he hear something once, you got it, Jerry.
And they got a, my dad didn't know what he was doing.

He was going to be a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a band. And then they got a, my dad's man, by the name of old man Martinez, he took the band over after he got a, and Gilbert, before he left, he bought a whole lot of orchestration. You know, you want to set up band with that. So they had the same Sonny Henry playing the trombone. And they practiced and practiced and practiced. So they asked me to play one day. I don't know if Sonny wasn't there. And now I take them, play the trombone and pieces and I went right along with them, with the pieces, you know. So I had been playing, I had been playing the local show and all them, all them places that I got that, that music was, I was, you, you, you be sharp when you, when you keep up there, you're, it's nothing, nothing, actually you're, it's nowhere. So when I went there, they told me that, they kept me on the trombone. And we had an orchestra and a march band, you see, the concert band. And we played with them and again what you call a layout, you see, dance like, and, well, they had, they're taking two bands and they had another bunch, they had an orchestra and we would take two and playing. And we had a piece, we had practice and they didn't know we had practice. I think I was a camellia, uh, what's up, Amelia, I don't care what it is, Cecilia, something like that. I don't know, I don't know, I don't know, I don't know, I don't know, I don't know, I don't know, I don't know.
What's the name, but the name's not again?

Yeah, so we had that. Delia. And late at night, the fella that we was playing, we put that up, you know, and we played that number. It ain't so easy neither when you get rid of honey, no. We played that number and, and why did y'all get that from, why did y'all get that piece from? We had been rehearsed in the dance, it was a nice dance number. But you got to know your business on them numbers. And they played some nice numbers too, you know, and they got mixed up on a number, they were trying to play a jazz number, you know, and the fella had been drinking and he picked it up in the wrong key. And I tell you, that was a mess. That was a, that was a really mess.
What was the name of Vanneken?
Huh?
What was the name? What was the name of that tool again? How do you spell that? Delia. Yeah.
That's a nice number. I don't know. I don't know. Oh yeah.
Well it was very popular. I'll get you the music sometime. He brought up plenty of popular numbers, you know.
And we came up with that and we did.
How late did you stay in music? When did you retire from music?

Oh, the sickness. I had what they call a tumor. Broke out on my hip. And it got graduated, graduated to about a year or so. It got put in as big as a baseball. And then my blood was bad. Now that, I had got a test about six months, less than six months. I went, it was negative. And I got another test. It was positive. So, the nurse said, well I got a test the first time. I said, it can't be. I said, we're taking your blood test and this. And so, they took it again and they told me, yeah, it was bad. Well I had to get treatment, you see. I had to get treatment and I had that tumor growing out on my leg. And that hindered me in the watch. I was in the WPA band. Well I was stuck around in there a good while. For as the last, I just had to give it up. It didn't last long after. I only left two tramboyant plays when I was Sonny Henry and the fellow by the name of Arthur. I only had two tramboyant plays left. Two of them left after you. And the band, this band, a little while. They didn't stay together too long after that. It went out. And I had to go on an operation. That would slow me up. And my instrument wasn't all that hot. You see, I needed another instrument. They came here many times. I came here and would go against my wood, you know. I asked them to play with them. And even Allen, they'd come tell me. He's running home in a jam. He said, come help me out. Well I'd go out there, but I couldn't walk like I wanted. And I just told them, I said, look, make this the last one. I said, I ain't making no more. So I got operated on. I never did make no more parades. And my instrument wasn't good enough for me to, I needed a new instrument. And at that time, it was tight, tough. Yeah, that's right. Tough to get a new instrument. My teeth was bad. I had to get my teeth fixed. I had to get that first. I couldn't get both of them. I just give it up and told them, no, no, I would come for them. And I got a ring up. The people would ring me, you know, different musicians would come play, but I wouldn't go. I figured my health was better. I was on the way out then. And I kept the instrument in here until I went to play in church. Went to join the church and went to play in the choir. And I played in there.
Which church was that that had music and had a band?
In the choir, yeah. Which church was that? Plenty of them have.
I know some of them do here.
And then, oh, yeah. And there's a First Remission Baptist Church. I played with them.
Well, very Miss Matthews played in that church, didn't he?

Yeah, he played in the church. He owned a drum. I don't know if they had any other instruments or not. But the time won't have been good in there. I'd have them mute, you know, and sighting numbers when they'd play them, like an overture, as they call them, anthem, you know. And they'd play that or sighting part in any sounds nice.
Can you tell us anything about the music in the churches down at Magnolia? Did they have a church down there that you belonged to?
I wasn't joined up with the church at the time.
Did you hear any music down there in the churches ever from outside or any place there? Spirituals or?
Instrumental to me? Well, any kind.
Even singing. Spirituals or gospel songs. What kind of music did they have?
Oh, they didn't even have a piano. You know how to concert tracer, but they didn't even have a piano. No organ or piano? No organ or piano. No organ.
What would they sing? Huh?
Sing, yeah.
What kind of, what was the singing like? Would they sing hymns?

They sing with, like anthem like. Slower numbers? Then they would sing jubilee. They'd mix them in, you see. Just like to do that. They, I think they call them an anthem. They'd word it out. Then they'd sing them strings. Then they'd word it out again and sing some more, you know. I don't know how to call that.
What were the jubilee songs like? Were they fast, fast, beat?

Oh yeah. Sometime when they, when they, sometime they would start to clap their hands on the jubilee. Sometimes the sisters would shout, you know, just like a person would dance. Yeah. Yeah. That would, that would be, that would, that would be in, after preaching and things like that, they would get on these things. Then they had what they call a social. Sometime we would give a social, you know, and selling different things. Then they would sing hymn because they were on the churches and, and they'd be shouting or I don't know what they call it. It wasn't dancing, but soon they're dancing and I don't know what it is.
I don't know what it is. To change the subject, did Chris Kelly ever use two trumpets?
No. Not, not, not in one day.
Well what would you do when he'd blow you up like that? Yeah. What would you do when he'd blow you up?
Well he, he would notify me.
He, and he'd send them a hammer.
He'd send a, he'd send somebody with me and he'd go on another job where he had deposit on a, on them jobs, you see.
Who did he send in this place?

Well he'd pick up just who he could get, what he could, somebody he could cheat. See, he'd take, he'd take that job, he'd be done, got, I'd be done, get him a deposit on a job, you know. And he'd take another job, you see. And he'd take another band and get a trumpet player and send with me. Sometimes he'd send a good one, sometimes he'd just send somebody not used to playing with the band. Well that's what got me disgusted.
Did y'all ever make any records with Chris? No, no. And who was in the rhythm section with Chris?

Well we had a fellow called, he living here, got one of them living here. At that time, a fellow used to call Teet. Well a Creole just called him Teet, you know, but I can't think of his other name now, but I know his other name too. He's alive now?
Huh? He's alive? No, he died. He died. And what did he play?

Bass. And a fellow by the name of T-Boy, he played banjo. And they were good. We had so many different, we changed them in so many different times. We had a fellow by the name of Mitchell. He was good on that, take the back of the bow and pick. That's before they started picking with the thumb.
They hit with the back of the bow?

No, the pop with your hole like this. Yeah. They take that, and them dudes could play that. That's where it started. That's the way it started right here at the fellow. That's where it started right here in the city. Used to pick it with that back part of the handle.
That's true. With the handle.

That's true, yeah. Then they tried, started with this. Some fellows used to put, the hand gets sold, they used to put tape on it. All that started right here in New Orleans. They didn't hear of it or, that's where they started. That's where the rhythms started coming in. There was double timing on it. You see, before they used to whoop, whoop, whoop, whoop, whoop, what did they cut that out? And they start that. And this other fellow used to start doubling time with the back of the bow, you see. That was probably by the name of Chester, I believe. He was the bestest they had on that. I was thinking about the man to start that too.
Is he alive, Chester?
I don't know, he's alive, but I haven't seen him and forget. Chester Lazard?
Huh?
Bass player. What's his last name, do you remember?
No.

Not Chester Lazard, huh? Is Chester Lazard a bass player? Mm-hmm. Little short guy. Chester Lazard is Chester Lazard, they call him. I ain't seen him for years. Used to work with Buddy Petit. That must be him.
Little short pedal, real short.
Yeah.
That's where the rhythm and thing started out.
Good drummers? Did they have good drummers in those days?
Oh yeah, they had what you call right time drummers.

See, when we first started from Johnny Brown, with Johnny Brown we had a drummer by the name of Faisal. He died early and then we got a fella by the name of Dave. Now I can't think of his last name right now, he had a brother called Ernest. Duck Ernest?
Hmm? Duck Ernest was his brother?
Duck Ernest was his brother, yeah. Half of different fathers.
Duck played bass? Yeah.

Well he must be Dave Ernest. Dave was a good drummer too, Dave was. He had to be good because he had to really, he changed him up if he wasn't good. That is, you have to keep that rhythm, you can't increase, you don't want no drummer going to increase, you don't want no drummer going to lag. You got to be right on the beat, you know? Like that, you play more easy, it's more easy on everybody. You get some drummers, they, they kind of lag just a section or a fraction of you, just keep, they drag you back, you see? Mm-hm. We started hitting our foot there with no reason to come up on that drum a little bit. And if he had to keep it going, I would get rid of him. He couldn't lag. All that started right here in the city. Putting a little more to it, a little more to it. And I think I could, with the chamber, not bragging on myself, I could play a whole lot of them. I could play, by playing the trumpet and had talent for music, I could put a whole lot in that, in the piece, you see, like that.
Before a tape runs out, what were some of the other tunes Buddy Bowling played?
Well, I couldn't think of all of them because it didn't have no name, you know? It didn't have no name.
I thought maybe you knew some of the different parts in him or something that he would have.
And he was, he was but going out when I come here, you see? He was passing.
Do you have your instrument now?
It's on my step, it's back there. I got runned over, you know? I've been playing the choir now. I got it out, I just throw it out in the shed.
You come with the old combo. You just...
What about your baritone?
Yeah, baritone too.
I didn't, I used to have a bar to baritone. The last time I played baritone, I played for three job with it. I had to borrow John Porter's baritone.
You just played for the choir just yourself, there was no band, there was just yourself accompaniment.
Yes, yeah, yeah. After I joined the church, well, I was just taking on with them. And they seemed to like it too. Yeah, I bet it was good.
Who was the first person you ever made a record for? When was that?
I didn't make no record until I made one with a brass band down there.
Yeah. With George Lewis? Yeah.
Oh, I see.
Yeah.

They didn't have much of a bass on them. The fellas just jumped up and made them records, you know? They didn't practice. The bass player, he didn't have no amateur. They had no bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo

segments.title: Opening and country club dance jobs, 1923-27
segments.summary: Brief opening about his birth date, then Barnes describes the high-class country club and carnival jobs he played in the 1920s.

segments.title: Robichaux band and Susquehanna lake excursion boat
segments.summary: Played Saturdays at the country club and ran dance excursions on the Susquehanna across the lake from West End.

segments.title: Antoine dance and the unfamiliar piece Robichaux produced
segments.summary: A ten-piece band at Antoine plays a request from Robichaux's music bundle; the requester turns out to be a guest from a rival band.

segments.title: Private dance at Arnaud's and the ten-dollar pay
segments.summary: Questions about the private party job, hours and pay of ten dollars, and the layout of the place.

segments.title: Barnes's brothers and sister and their instruments
segments.summary: He names his brothers Thomas, Freddie and Alfred, their ages and instruments, and a sister who played nothing.

segments.title: Playing trumpet with a C-trombone orchestra by holding down the third valve
segments.summary: At a country dance his brothers' E-flat clarinets did not match the local band, so he transposed by keeping a valve held down.

segments.title: Plantation bells and the field work day
segments.summary: Describes the plantation bell schedule, the working day, and his father as foreman.

segments.title: Plantation pay, laying off rows and deciding to leave for the city
segments.summary: He explains skilled field work at 85 cents a day, a miserable day plowing in water, and why he decided to leave.

segments.title: What became of the plantation and whether city bands visited
segments.summary: The plantation is now overgrown and flooded; no city bands came, only their own country band.

segments.title: Members of Henry Allen's and the Excelsior band
segments.summary: Asked to name Henry Allen's band members, he recalls the drummers including Yance and says Clay Giles was in a different band.

segments.title: Hearing Dusen, Farnish and excursion bands, and Alexander's Ragtime Band
segments.summary: He heard Dusen and Farnish only in the city; excursion bands were the big music at home, where he first heard Alexander's Ragtime Band.

segments.title: Hearing Buddy Bolden at Congo Square on a visit
segments.summary: Bolden was on his way out; he heard him and other bands outside Globe Hall at the square.

segments.title: Magnolia band in the Tenth of May parade
segments.summary: The country band came to the city parade in white coats, played all day, and he talks about a musician who dropped dead and about Chris Kelly living nearby.

segments.title: Playing a Bolden tune through the district and tune names
segments.summary: Passing through the district the country band played a Bolden piece to applause; he discusses unnamed band tunes and the Lizard on the Rail hit.

segments.title: Frankie Dusen could not read music
segments.summary: Barnes doubts Dusen taught bands since he could not read, recalling him in the WPA band.

segments.title: Who played with Bolden and Barnes's impressions of him
segments.summary: He recalls Cornish with Bolden, that Bolden had lost his mind by then, and contrasts Bolden's strong sound with Manuel Perez.

segments.title: Photographs of the Magnolia band and Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Whether pictures exist of old bands; photographers snapped them at the train stop but never delivered pictures.

segments.title: Country bands versus city bands, reading and playing by ear
segments.summary: He thinks the country bands were better than bigger-name city bands, a view confirmed when he taught musicians in the WPA band.

segments.title: Joining the Ninth Ward parade band under Gilbert and Martinez
segments.summary: Sonny Henry recommended him to the band; Gilbert tested players with sight music, Martinez took over, and he describes a rehearsal and the tune Delia.

segments.title: Illness ending his playing career
segments.summary: A tumor and bad blood forced him out of the WPA band.

segments.title: Church music, in the city and at Magnolia
segments.summary: Churches he played with, and the unaccompanied hymns, anthems and jubilee singing at the plantation church.

segments.title: Chris Kelly double-booking jobs and sending substitutes
segments.summary: Kelly took deposits on two jobs and sent a substitute trumpeter, which disgusted Barnes.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's rhythm section and the origin of banjo and bass styles
segments.summary: He names Teet on bass, T-Boy on banjo, Mitchell, and Chester Lazard, and describes picking with the back of the bow and double timing as a New Orleans development.

segments.title: Drummers and keeping steady time
segments.summary: Drummers with Johnny Brown including Faisal and Dave Ernest, and why a drummer must not lag or rush.

segments.title: Tunes Buddy Bolden played
segments.summary: Barnes cannot name Bolden's unnamed tunes; Bolden was passing out when he arrived.

segments.title: His instruments and playing for the church choir
segments.summary: His horn and baritone are put away, and he now plays alone to accompany the choir.

segments.title: First recording with a brass band
segments.summary: His only recording was with a brass band, apparently with George Lewis, made with little rehearsal.
